title: Midterm Reckoning: UK Local Elections Could Redraw Political Map as Starmer Fights for Survival
summary: On Thursday, millions of British voters headed to the polls in local and regional elections that could fundamentally reshape the country's political landscape—and potentially end Keir Starmer's premiership less than two years after his Labour Party's landslide victory. With about 5,000 council seats and several mayoralties up for grabs across England, plus devolved parliaments in Scotland and Wales, the vote is widely seen as a midterm verdict on Starmer's troubled leadership. Starmer's approval ratings have plummeted amid a series of missteps. His government has struggled to deliver on promises of economic growth and improved public services, a task complicated by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, which has disrupted oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. Perhaps most damaging was his appointment of Peter Mandelson—a figure tarnished by association with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein—as ambassador to Washington. The move triggered a crisis in February, when some Labour lawmakers, including the party's Scottish leader, urged Starmer to resign. Labour is defending roughly 2,500 council seats, and party insiders fear significant losses. A rout could embolden rivals such as Health Secretary Wes Streeting, former Deputy Prime Minister Angela Rayner, or Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham to mount a leadership challenge. Even if Starmer survives, many analysts doubt he will lead Labour into the next general election, due by 2029. But the story extends beyond Labour's woes. Luke Tryl of pollster More in Common said the elections could mark "the total collapse of the traditional two-party system" that has long been dominated by Labour and the Conservatives. The hard-right Reform UK, led by Nigel Farage, is targeting working-class, former Labour strongholds with an anti-establishment, anti-immigration message. The Green Party is also poised to make substantial gains in urban and university areas. Both parties have faced increased scrutiny: Farage is under fire for failing to declare a £5 million donation from a cryptocurrency billionaire, while the Greens have fired several candidates over antisemitic social media posts. The Conservatives, the main opposition, are also expected to lose ground, with the centrist Liberal Democrats picking up some seats. "Labour's going to lose to Reform in some places, Greens in others, and here and there they'll lose one or two seats to the Liberal Democrats and the Conservatives as well," said Tony Travers, a professor at the London School of Economics. "They're fighting on four fronts in England—five in Wales and Scotland." Farage declared on the eve of the vote that a strong Reform showing would mean Starmer is "gone by the middle of summer." As results trickle in, the political future of the UK hangs in the balance.
why_it_matters: If the two-party system fractures, future governments might become unstable coalitions, affecting everything from university fees to climate policy—decisions that will directly shape the world you will inherit.

background_read: Keir Starmer, a former human rights lawyer, became Prime Minister in 2024 after Labour’s landslide victory ended 14 years of Conservative rule, winning 403 seats in the House of Commons.
The UK’s devolved parliaments—the Scottish Parliament in Edinburgh and the Senedd in Cardiff—control matters like education, health, and transport, so their elections are vital to national politics.
The Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea passage between Iran and Oman, is a critical shipping lane for about one-fifth of the world’s oil tankers, making it a flashpoint in global conflicts.
Peter Mandelson, the new ambassador to Washington, is a divisive figure who modernised the Labour Party in the 1990s but has faced criticism over past ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
UK local councils manage services such as garbage collection, schools, and social care, and their midterm elections often signal the national mood.

perspectives.description: Reform UK and Green Party supporters see this as a chance to break the Labour-Conservative duopoly, giving a voice to those who feel ignored. If they gain enough seats, they could force the major parties to adopt more radical policies on immigration, the environment, or economic fairness.

Critics argue a fragmented vote could lead to weak, indecisive governance, with extremist voices gaining influence. The scandals surrounding Reform and the Greens raise questions about candidate vetting and the integrity of these movements.

Midterm local elections historically punish incumbents and preview future general election trends. The real test is whether the collapse of the two-party system is a permanent realignment or a temporary protest vote against current leadership.

The outcome might pressure Starmer to resign or trigger a snap general election, potentially ushering in a multi-party era. How the next prime minister navigates the economic fallout of the Iran war and rebuilds trust could define British politics for a generation.
